There is a book floating around on Ebay called "Abraham Lincoln and the Sleeping Sentinel of Vermont" by Waldo Glover printed sometime in the 1930's.  I got a copy from my cousin's lady friend who got it there.  It is probably the most accurate description of this tale of the boy solider from the backwoods of a small town.  The incident happened at the very beginning of the war when union posts flanked Washington and posted guards around the Southern part of the Potomac river  in an effort to guard against a possible Confederate invasion of the capitol.  Scott was with the 3rd Vermont volunteers as I recall, one of the first to actively participate in the war effort.  Vermont regiments like all regiments at that time were very closely knit in an unfamiliar place, far from home.  Nobody really knows why he fell asleep.  Covering for a sick comrade was one thought.  Others suggest that most of the northern recruits were subject to dysentery from the swampy marshlands that surrounded Washington (Trump's SWAMP).  When you don't feel well, you sleep alot.  But then the story gets muddied by all the attention it brought about.  It was the first propaganda story from the war similar to the Jessica Lynch story at the onset of the Iraq war and drummed up support for the war during the very beginning of the conflict.  There was a long poem written about the Scott case that was published and recited at events and public gatherings. Most people were very critical of executing him.  His execution would have brought unfavorable attention to the Union cause that had just begun and needed support from Americans.  The NYT, the Boston Herald and newspapers in Vermont carried stories about the incident.  (In the 20's there was a radio drama written about Scott and Lincoln).  As Wikipedia says, its unlikely Lincoln personally visited the 3rd VT at the Chain bridge where they were stationed.. He more than likely wrote the pardon at the urgings of Chittenden, another Vermonter who was a close aide to the President.  It is more likely that the general commanding the VT brigade (another Vermonter) wanted to make a lesson from Scott's failure on guard duty and scare hell out of the troops by setting him up for the execution. They brought him out that morning and had selected a group of 4 to fire at him.  They pinned a white circle of cloth on his blouse and 3 were given blanks and 1 had an active bullet. At the last moment, the pardon issued by Lincoln was read and he was released.  The following spring, he took part in McClellen's failed Peninsula campaign and was killed while carrying another soldier away from a futile attempt to rush a Confederate fortification surrounded by a swamp.  Scott took 5 or more bullets. He never would have said anything since he was unconscious after receiving the bullet wounds until his death the next day.  Whatever happened, it was more myth than reality but made for a good story and helped the war effort.  My Dad's side of the family claims to be related to the Scott family but I've never found the connection in all my research.
